questions.prompt: What does mutual TLS (mTLS) add on top of standard TLS?
options: The client also presents a certificate, which the server validates before the connection is considered authenticated
It encrypts traffic more strongly than standard TLS, using a longer key
It removes the need for a certificate authority entirely
It only applies to connections made from a mobile device
It replaces OAuth as the identity layer for all Salesforce integrations
It allows a self-signed certificate to be trusted automatically by any server
questions.explain: Standard TLS is one-way: the client verifies the server's certificate. Mutual TLS adds the missing half, requiring the client to also present a certificate the server validates before the connection completes.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is wrong because mTLS isn't about stronger encryption or longer keys -- it's about adding a second direction of identity verification. TLS and mTLS can use the same encryption strength; the difference is purely about whether the client, not just the server, has to prove who it is.

questions.prompt: A nightly middleware job syncs inventory data with no user present, and the team wants to avoid managing certificates. Which OAuth flow fits best, and what single setting on the connected app determines everything that job is allowed to do?
options: Client Credentials flow; the connected app's configured 'Run As' user determines what the integration can do
Authorization Code flow; a refresh token determines what the integration can do
JWT Bearer flow; the uploaded certificate determines what the integration can do
Username-Password flow; the integration's IP range determines what it can do
questions.explain: No human is present (ruling out Authorization Code) and certificates are to be avoided (ruling out JWT Bearer), leaving Client Credentials flow -- where the Run As user's permissions are the real boundary on what the integration can do.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Named Credentials and External Credentials.
options: An External Credential holds the authentication protocol and principals; a Named Credential holds the callout endpoint and points at an External Credential
One External Credential can be reused across multiple Named Credentials that call different endpoints on the same system
A principal is automatically available to every user in the org once it's created
Which permission sets a principal is associated with determines who can use it in a callout
Named Credentials make Apex code's callout authentication visible to anyone who can read that Apex class
questions.explain: External Credentials hold the authentication configuration (reusable across endpoints); Named Credentials hold the specific endpoint. A principal isn't open to everyone -- it's gated by permission-set association, which is the opposite of being automatically available or exposing the credential to Apex code.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the ________ OAuth flow is the right choice when an individual human must explicitly log in through a browser and consent before an integration can access their data.
questions.explain: Authorization Code flow is built around a human explicitly logging in and approving the connected app -- the only one of the three integration flows covered in this course that assumes a consenting human is present.

questions.prompt: Match each Named Credential principal type to the scenario it fits.
left: A scheduled, unattended ETL job with no individual user context
An integration where the external system must enforce access by the actual human behind each request
right: A single, shared identity used for every user whose code triggers the callout
Each Salesforce user authenticates to the external system with their own individual credential
questions.explain: Named Principal is one shared identity for everyone, which fits an unattended service-style job. Per-User gives each individual their own credential, which fits a case where the external system needs to recognize and restrict each specific human.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the JWT Bearer OAuth flow in the correct order.
items: The integration signs a JWT using its private key
The integration sends the signed JWT to Salesforce's token endpoint
Salesforce validates the JWT's signature against the certificate uploaded to the connected app
Salesforce returns an access token the integration can use for API calls
questions.explain: JWT Bearer flow runs sign, send, validate, then issue: the integration signs its own token with a private key only it holds, Salesforce checks that signature against the public certificate already on file, and only then issues the access token -- with no browser step anywhere in the sequence.

questions.prompt: An integration user has the API Only setting enabled and a narrowly-scoped permission set, and its credential is later exposed in a leaked config file. What is the practical effect of API Only in this situation?
options: The exposed credential still can't be used to log into the Salesforce UI and browse around -- it's confined to whatever the API and the permission set allow
API Only automatically revokes the credential the moment it's used from an unfamiliar IP
API Only prevents the credential from being used at all, even for API calls
API Only has no effect once a credential is exposed; it only matters at initial setup
questions.explain: API Only closes off the UI login path specifically. Even with the credential exposed, whoever has it still can't log into the UI -- they're limited to the API surface the permission set defines, which is a smaller blast radius than a full UI session would allow.

questions.prompt: Why does this course recommend against pointing a new integration at a real employee's existing Salesforce login?
options: The integration's access and reliability become tied to that employee's own role changes, password resets, or departure, and incident attribution becomes ambiguous
Salesforce technically blocks API calls made under a human user's standard login
Employee logins cannot be granted the API Enabled permission
It is only a cost issue, since human user licenses are more expensive than integration user licenses
questions.explain: A dedicated integration user decouples the integration's identity and access from any one human's employment status or access changes, and keeps 'who did this' unambiguous if something goes wrong -- the actual reasons this course gives, not a licensing or technical API restriction.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about scoping access for an API-based integration.
options: Going through the API inherits the calling user's existing object- and field-level access rather than using a separate, looser rulebook
A connected app's OAuth scope can narrow what an issued token is used for, but it can never grant access beyond the underlying user's actual permissions
Granting an integration user the System Administrator profile is good practice because it avoids future support tickets
The API Enabled permission must be granted before a user can make any API call at all
OAuth scope and the underlying user's permission set are interchangeable; configuring either one alone is always sufficient
questions.explain: The API inherits the user's own access rather than defining a separate rulebook, and OAuth scope only narrows (never widens) what the underlying user's permissions already allow. API Enabled is a hard precondition for any API call. System Administrator as a default is explicitly the over-scoping mistake this course warns against, and scope/permission set are not interchangeable -- both need to be set deliberately.

questions.prompt: Under what condition does a Protected Custom Metadata Type actually hide its data from other orgs, per Salesforce's own documentation?
options: Only when used inside a managed package -- outside a package it behaves like a public custom metadata type
Always, regardless of whether it's packaged
Only when Shield Platform Encryption is also enabled on the org
Only when the record is also marked read-only
Only if the org has fewer than 10 million custom metadata records
Protected Custom Metadata Types cannot store secrets of any kind
questions.explain: Salesforce's own Apex documentation states that protected custom metadata types only behave as protected inside a managed package; outside one, they behave like public types, readable by every profile including the guest user.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the common misconception this course specifically corrects: many developers assume 'protected' means hidden everywhere, but the protection is conditional on the managed-package context, not automatic in every org.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ is the Salesforce mechanism that tracks configuration changes -- who modified a permission set, a connected app's policy, or a Named Credential's settings, and when -- as distinct from event monitoring's focus on data and API activity.
questions.explain: Setup Audit Trail answers 'who changed how this integration is configured to behave,' a different axis from event monitoring, which answers what the integration's identity actually did once configured that way.

questions.prompt: Match each IP-related Salesforce control to what it actually does.
left: Enforce login IP ranges on every request
right: Blocks login attempts from outside the defined range
Skips the extra identity-verification challenge for logins from listed addresses, without blocking anything by itself
Governs whether a specific connected app's OAuth traffic is bound by the org's IP restrictions
Extends the Login IP Range check beyond login to every subsequent request
questions.explain: Login IP Range actually blocks; Trusted IP Range only skips a verification challenge; Connected App IP Relaxation is a separate per-app dial; and the 'every request' session setting extends enforcement beyond the initial login to the whole session.

questions.prompt: An admin relaxes a connected app's IP restrictions to fix a failing integration that uses the JWT Bearer flow. Why might this not actually solve the problem?
options: JWT Bearer and SAML Bearer flows always enforce IP restrictions regardless of the connected app's relaxation setting, so the integration's source IP still has to fall within the applicable Login IP Range or Trusted IP Range
Connected app IP relaxation settings only take effect after 72 hours
JWT Bearer flow does not support connected apps at all
IP relaxation settings can only be configured by Salesforce Support, not by an admin
questions.explain: This is the specific exception this course flags: JWT Bearer and SAML Bearer always enforce IP restrictions no matter what the connected app's relaxation policy says, so the lever the admin just pulled doesn't apply to this flow at all.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about historical event log data versus real-time event monitoring.
options: Historical event log data becomes queryable only after a processing delay and is retained for a limited window
Real-time event monitoring streams events as they happen, suited to detecting something unusual close to when it occurs
The two are fully interchangeable, so a program only needs one or the other
A documented baseline of normal activity is needed before either kind of event data is useful for spotting abnormal activity
Setup Audit Trail and event monitoring track the exact same information
questions.explain: Historical and real-time event data serve different purposes and aren't interchangeable -- a program relying on only one will miss either timely detection or complete retrospective review. Either kind of event data also needs a documented baseline to be useful. Setup Audit Trail tracks configuration changes, a different thing entirely from event monitoring's data/API activity focus.

questions.prompt: Put these three passes of a structured integration security review in the order this course presents them.
items: Configuration pass -- Named Credential setup, certificate expiry, IP range accuracy, connected app policy
Identity pass -- the integration user's actual granted access versus what the integration currently does, API Only status, ownership currency
Monitoring pass -- whether event monitoring and Setup Audit Trail are actually being watched, and whether the documented baseline still matches current activity
questions.explain: The review walks configuration, then identity, then monitoring -- checking what's set up, who/what is acting and with what access, and finally whether anyone would actually notice a problem.

questions.prompt: A public Apex REST endpoint computes an HMAC signature over a JSON payload that has been deserialized and then re-serialized before the comparison, instead of over the original raw request body. What is the risk this course specifically flags about this implementation?
options: Re-serialization can change whitespace or key order, which can silently break a signature check that was actually valid for the original bytes
HMAC signatures cannot be computed on JSON payloads under any circumstances
This approach is slower but otherwise has no correctness risk
Re-serialization automatically strips the signature header from the request
questions.explain: The signature was computed over specific original bytes. Checking it against a reconstructed version of the payload can fail even for a genuinely legitimate request, which is why this course recommends computing the HMAC over the raw request body.

questions.prompt: In the Meridian Parts case study, why did 'the endpoint URL isn't published anywhere' fail to actually protect the inbound integration?
options: Because Salesforce Site URLs are discoverable regardless of whether they're advertised, making this a case of security through obscurity rather than a real control
Because the researcher was a former Meridian employee with insider knowledge of the URL
Because Salesforce Sites cannot host custom Apex REST endpoints
Because the signature verification on the endpoint was misconfigured, not missing
questions.explain: An unpublished URL is not the same as a secret -- Site URLs are discoverable, which is exactly why relying on obscurity instead of signature verification left Meridian's endpoint exposed.

questions.prompt: Select every control gap this course identifies in the Meridian Parts case study.
options: No signature verification on the inbound endpoint
A guest user profile cloned from an existing, broader profile instead of scoped to the endpoint's actual needs
A Username-Password flow credential for a System Administrator-profile user, hardcoded into a middleware config screen and never rotated for three years
The outbound integration correctly used the JWT Bearer flow with a properly scoped Run As user
No IP restriction on either direction, and no named owner or monitoring after the original contractor left
questions.explain: Meridian's gaps span inbound (unverified endpoint, over-broad guest profile), outbound (wrong flow, hardcoded and unrotated System Administrator credential), and operational (no IP restriction, no owner, no monitoring) -- the outbound integration was never correctly scoped; that option inverts what actually happened.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when answering an architect review-board scenario question, a defensible answer names the specific ________ in the scenario's wording that rules out each plausible-but-wrong alternative, rather than just asserting the chosen answer.
questions.explain: The reusable structure this course teaches is to identify every stated constraint and explain which one eliminates each alternative -- that's what separates a defensible architectural answer from a confident guess.

questions.prompt: Match each integration scenario to the OAuth flow this course recommends for it.
left: An unattended nightly ERP sync with no human present, team wants to avoid certificates
A multi-tenant SaaS product where each customer must explicitly consent before any data flows
A field-service mobile app where each technician logs in with their own credentials to act as themselves
A server-to-server integration where a certificate is already available and no shared secret should exist in any config screen
questions.explain: No human present plus wanting to avoid certificates points to Client Credentials. Explicit per-customer consent points to Authorization Code. A human logging in individually to act as themselves is also Authorization Code, just in its per-user-login shape. A certificate already available with no shared secret desired points to JWT Bearer.

questions.prompt: Put these four steps of this course's reusable scenario-answering structure in order.
items: Identify every constraint stated in the scenario's wording
For each plausible answer, name the specific constraint that rules it out
State the recommendation and connect it directly back to the constraints that survived
Note any remaining risk or follow-up action the recommendation doesn't fully resolve on its own
questions.explain: This four-step structure -- identify constraints, rule out alternatives, justify the surviving recommendation, then flag remaining risk -- is what this course teaches as the difference between a confident-sounding guess and a defensible architectural answer.

questions.prompt: A review finds two issues on the same integration: a slightly stale monitoring baseline, and a public inbound endpoint with no signature verification at all. Per this course's remediation-ordering guidance, which should generally be prioritized first?
options: The unverified public inbound endpoint, since it's actively exploitable by anyone who finds the URL, versus a baseline that's only somewhat out of date
The stale monitoring baseline, since monitoring issues always take priority over configuration issues
Neither -- both should be left until the next scheduled review cycle
They are equally urgent and should be fixed in whatever order is most convenient
questions.explain: This course's default ordering (from the Meridian Parts case study and the checklist lesson) ranks actively exploitable gaps -- like an unverified public endpoint -- above issues like a slightly stale baseline, which reduce detection speed but aren't themselves an open door.
